description: Long open A, like 'father' but purer and never gliding into another vowel.
tip: A vowel is long before h, before a doubled vowel, or before a single consonant.

description: Short open A, cut off quickly.
tip: A vowel is short before a doubled consonant: Mann, kann, Stadt.

description: Long closed E, close to English 'say' but with no y-glide at the end.
tip: Keep your jaw still — German long vowels do not slide.

description: Short open E, like 'bed'.
tip: Contrast Beet [eː] with Bett [ɛ] — length changes the word.

description: Long EE, as in 'see'.
tip: The spelling ie is almost always this long sound, not two vowels.

description: Short I, as in 'sit'.
tip: Shorter and laxer than English — do not let it drift toward 'ee'.

description: Long closed O, rounded, without the English w-glide.
tip: Round your lips before you start the sound and hold them still.

description: Short open O, as in British 'hot'.
tip: Common before doubled consonants: Sonne, kommen, Sommer.

description: Long OO, as in 'food', strongly rounded.
tip: Push your lips well forward — German rounding is tighter than English.

description: Short U, as in 'put'.
tip: Relax the lips slightly compared with the long [uː].

description: Long open Ä, a stretched 'e' as in 'air'.
tip: Many speakers merge this with [eː]; both are widely accepted.

description: Long Ö — no English equivalent.
tip: Say [eː] as in 'gehen', then round your lips without moving your tongue.

description: Short Ö, the clipped counterpart of [øː].
tip: Say [ɛ] as in 'Bett', then round the lips.

description: Long Ü — the classic hard German vowel.
tip: Say [iː] as in 'Liebe', hold your tongue still, and round your lips into a whistle.

description: Short Ü, the clipped counterpart of [yː].
tip: Say [ɪ] as in 'Kind', then round the lips.

description: Diphthong like English 'eye'.
tip: Remember: ei sounds like the English letter I; ie sounds like E.

description: Diphthong like English 'house'.
tip: Starts open and closes into a rounded u.

description: Diphthong like English 'boy'.
tip: eu and äu are pronounced identically — Häuser rhymes with Kreuzer.

description: Unstressed final -er becomes a vowel close to 'uh'.
tip: Never pronounce a hard English R here — Vater ends like 'fah-tuh'.

description: Soft ch after i, e, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu, l, n, r and in -chen.
tip: Whisper a strong English 'h' in 'hue' — do not substitute 'sh'.

description: Hard ch after a, o, u, au.
tip: Like Scottish 'loch', made further back in the throat.

description: Like English 'sh', with firmer lip rounding.
tip: Distinct from [ç]: Kirche [ç] versus Kirsche [ʃ].

description: Initial sp is pronounced 'shp'.
tip: Only at the start of a word or stem — Wespe keeps a plain s.

description: Initial st is pronounced 'sht'.
tip: Same rule as sp-: stem-initial only, so Fenster keeps a plain s.

description: S before a vowel is voiced, like English 'z'.
tip: Sie starts like 'zee', not 'see'.

description: Voiceless S. ß follows a long vowel or diphthong, ss a short one.
tip: Straße has a long a; Fluss has a short u.

description: w is pronounced like English v; v is usually pronounced like English f.
tip: The letters swap round compared with English — Wein sounds like 'vine'.

description: Always 'ts', never English 'z'.
tip: Zeit sounds like 'tsait'. Final -b, -d, -g devoice similarly: Hund ends in 't'.
